'''Henry Babcock Veatch Jr.''' (September 26, 1911 &ndash; July 9, 1999) was an American philosopher, known as one of the "leading [[Aristotelianism#Meta-ontology|neo-Aristotelian]] philosophers of the twentieth century".<ref name=OLL>{{cite web|accessdate=July 13, 2025 |url=https://oll.libertyfund.org/people/henry-b-veatch
|title=Henry B. Veatch (1911 – 1999)|publisher=The Online Library of Liberty (OLL)}}</ref>

==Life and career==
Henry Babcock Veatch Jr. was born on September 26, 1911, in [[Evansville, Indiana|Evansville]], [[Indiana]]. He attended [[Phillips Exeter Academy]] in [[Exeter, New Hampshire]].<ref name=JSTOR/>  He then attended [[Harvard University]], where he received his [[Bachelor of Arts|A.B.]] ''([[summa cum laude]])'' (1932), [[Master of Arts|M.A.]] degree (1933), and a [[Ph.D.]] (1937). Following his Ph.D. he pursued post-doctoral studies at [[Heidelberg University]] in Germany, where he studied with [[Alfred North Whitehead]], [[Karl Jaspers]], [[Henry M. Sheffer]], [[C. I. Lewis]], [[R. B. Perry]], and [[A. O. Lovejoy]].<ref name=JSTOR/>

Veatch came to the Philosophy Department at [[Indiana University]] (IU) as an instructor in 1937. He was named assistant professor in 1941 and full professor in 1952. While at Indiana University, Veatch received many awards and honors. In 1954, he became the first recipient of the Frederick Bachman Lieber Award for Distinguished  Teaching. He was popular with his students and was awarded the [[Sigma Delta Chi]] "Brown Derby" Award for most popular professor. In 1961, Veatch was named Distinguished Service Professor.<ref name="Veatchpapers">{{cite web|accessdate=July 13, 2025 |url=https://archives.iu.edu/catalog/InU-Ar-VAA2654 |title=Henry Babcock Veatch papers, 1941-1997|work= Collection C163|publisher=Indiana University Archives |location=Bloomington, Indiana}}</ref>

In 1965, Veatch left IU for [[Northwestern University]] where he remained until 1973. He then went to [[Georgetown University]], where he was philosophy department chair from 1973 to 1976.<ref name="Veatchpapers" /> Veatch also had visiting professorships at [[Colby College]], [[Haverford College]] and [[St. Thomas University (New Brunswick)|St. Thomas University]]. In 1983, he retired as a distinguished professor and returned to [[Bloomington (Indiana)|Bloomington]].<ref name="Veatchpapers" />

Veatch was active in the [[Episcopal Church (United States)|Episcopal Church]] and served as president of the [[American Catholic Philosophical Association]]. He served as president of the [[Metaphysical Society of America]] in 1961. In 1970&ndash;71 he served as president of the Western Division of the [[American Philosophical Association]]. He was a member of the [[Guild of Scholars of The Episcopal Church]].

Henry Veatch died on July 9, 1999, in [[Bloomington (Indiana)|Bloomington]], [[Indiana]].  His death was within eight hours of his wife of
sixty years, Mary Jane Wilson Veatch. He was survived by two daughters and two grandsons.<ref name=JSTOR/>

Indiana University maintains the archive of his collected papers (1941&ndash;1997).<ref name="Veatchpapers"/>

==Philosophy==
Veatch was a major proponent of [[intellectualism]], an authority on [[Thomism|Thomistic philosophy]], and one of the leading neo-[[Aristotelianism|Aristotelian]] thinkers of his time.<ref name=OLL/>  He opposed such modern and contemporary developments as the "[[transcendental idealism|transcendental turn]]" and the "[[linguistic turn]]."  A staunch advocate of plain speaking and "[[Hoosier]]" common sense, in philosophy and elsewhere, he argued on behalf of [[philosophical realism|realist]] [[metaphysics]] and practical [[ethics]].<ref>Rocco Porecco and Ronald Duska, "Memorial Minutes: Henry Veatch 1911&ndash;1999," ''Proceedings and Addresses of the American Philosophical Association'', vol. 73, no. 2 (Nov/1999), pp. 31&ndash;2.</ref>

Veatch's most widely read book was ''Rational Man: A Modern Interpretation of Aristotelian Ethics'' (1962) which explicitly offered a rationalist counterpoint to [[William Barrett (philosopher)|William Barrett's]] well-known study in [[existentialism|existential philosophy]], ''[[Irrational Man]]'' (1958).

==Major works==
*''Concerning the Ontological Status of Logical Forms'' (1948)
*''Aristotelian and Mathematical Logic'' (1950)
*''In Defense of the Syllogism'' (1950)
*''Metaphysics and the Paradoxes'' (1952)
*''[[Intentional Logic|Intentional Logic: A Logic Based on Philosophical Realism]]'' (1952)
*''Realism and Nominalism Revisited'' (1954)
*''Logic as a Human Instrument'' (1959, with Francis Parker)
*''Rational Man: A Modern Interpretation of Aristotelian Ethics'' (1962)
*''The Truths of Metaphysics'' (1964)
*''Non-cognitivism in Ethics: A modest proposal for its diagnosis and cure'' (1966)
*''Two Logics: the Conflict between Classical and Neo-Analytic Philosophy'' (1969)
*''For an Ontology of Morals: A Critique of Contemporary Ethical Theory '' (1971)
*''Aristotle: A Contemporary Appreciation'' (1974)
*''Human Rights: Fact or Fancy'' (1985)
*''Swimming Against the Current in Contemporary Philosophy'' (1990)
